Chapter 5. Intentional Practices: Building Habits That Aim the Heart Toward God
You know, most people just sort of drift through life, shaped by habits they never really chose. The routines of work, the endless pull of technology, even the rhythms of our culture—they all form our hearts in ways we barely notice.
But if we want to grow spiritually, we can't just go with the flow. It takes intention. It means being willing to choose habits that point our desires in a better direction.
Picture a busy parent, juggling the demands of work and family. She's longing for some peace, for a sense of purpose, but finds herself trapped in this cycle of exhaustion and constant distraction. Then one day, she decides to carve out just a few minutes each morning for silence and prayer. At first, it feels strange—almost pointless. But as the days go by, that simple habit turns into a lifeline. It's a moment of stillness that begins to shape the rest of her day.
Or think about a group of friends who decide to share a meal every week. They put away their phones, light a candle, and take turns saying what they're grateful for. The ritual is so simple, but it creates a bond. It teaches them to slow down, to really listen, and to care for one another. That habit starts shaping their hearts too, guiding them to love their community more than just staying busy.
The thing is, these intentional practices aren’t about trying to earn something or just ticking off boxes. They're about forming the heart, training it to love what’s truly good. Habits like worship, prayer, gratitude, and serving others—they become the grooves where our desires naturally run.
Of course, building new habits isn’t easy. It takes patience, persistence, and a whole lot of grace. Some days, those old routines feel so much stronger. The heart might crave comfort or just another distraction. But if you stick with it, those new practices gradually sink in. They start forming new loves.
Spiritual formation—it’s a journey, not some final destination. It’s a process of becoming, of learning to love what’s really worth loving. The habits you choose—at home, at work, in your community—are the tools for this journey. They shape your heart, one small step at a time.
The world’s full of competing stories, each trying to sell its own version of the good life. But with intentional practices, you can actually form a different kind of heart—a heart that loves God, cares for neighbors, and finds real joy in the everyday.
That’s the quiet power of habit—the spiritual strength that comes from loving what’s truly good.
